steps.message: Reviewing the intake and the question.

claims.text: Goal entered: cut grid electricity 30% by 2030, with a $750,000 capital budget (budget year 2027) and outage backup for gym cooling, lighting and communications.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Scenario B (standard efficiency plus a budget-sized solar array of about 140 kW) is estimated to cut about 51% to 67% of annual grid use, which reaches the 30% goal even at the low end, and stays within the $750,000 budget. Simple payback, not a full financial model.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario A (efficiency only) is estimated to cut about 6% to 18% of annual use and does not reach the 30% goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C (deep efficiency, whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut about 93% to 100% of annual use and is the only scenario with outage backup (about 8 to 9 hours), but costs $105,950 to $686,661 more than the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Meeting the goal with outage backup may take more than the $750,000 set aside. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision once the gap is compared with the savings.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Red Hook Recreation Center (NYC Parks), 155 Bay Street, Brooklyn; park recreation center built 1936; flat roof; Con Edison service; floor area entered as 21,600 sq ft and roof area entered as 32,860 sq ft.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city lot record lists this lot under a different street, 140 Lorraine Street, while the address entered is 155 Bay Street. It may be another frontage of the same lot; confirm the address.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city lot record shows a gross floor area of 21,600 sq ft, one floor, a landmark flag, and a lot of 212,400 sq ft. The lot size does not match the floor area entered.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's Local Law 84 energy report (2024) shows 375,066 kWh (energy over time) of electricity, matching the annual use entered, but lists gross floor area as 27,069 sq ft (against 21,600 entered) and year built 1920 (against 1936). The entered 21,600 sq ft is kept as the working figure; please confirm which is right.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city's building footprints show four buildings on the lot totaling 32,862 sq ft of ground area (largest 27,000 sq ft). This matches the roof area entered, but a footprint is ground area, not a measured roof, and it includes all four buildings. The roof area stays the working figure and must be verified by an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar already exists: 11.4 kW (kW means how much power at one moment) is already installed, and the city's Local Law 24 record agrees, with an estimated 12,540 kWh a year. The plan sizes new solar only on the roof left free, and the baseline for the goal is the electricity the building buys from the grid, which this existing array already lowers.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The annual use of 375,066 kWh matches the city's reported electricity figure; it is treated as measured, though the intake does not say it came from uploaded bills.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A1: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around PVWatts' 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A2: usable roof setback factor of 0.55 (about 55% of the roof is treated as usable).
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A3: array density of 66 sq ft per kW DC.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A4: critical load not given, so estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft x 21,600 sq ft = 21.6 kW (a planning estimate, not metered). Backup length not given, so 8 hours assumed. Battery energy = kW x hours / 0.85 round-trip efficiency = 203 kWh.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A7: efficiency measures (LED and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: A9: planning-level benchmark prices, not quotes: solar $2,528-3,752 per kW DC, battery $546-812 per kWh, and efficiency cost per kWh saved per year of $1.17-4.02 (standard) and $1.09-3.83 (deep), from the middle half of completed NYC projects (NYSERDA data); standard efficiency saving 10-20% and deep 15-25% are planning estimates, and only 62%-88% of them is counted because the City's audited projects delivered that share.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Baseline: 375,066 kWh a year of electricity bought from the grid, after the existing 11.4 kW of solar.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city energy report also shows 3,073,752 thousand BTU (kBtu) of natural gas, so heating is largely gas. Gas heating is outside an electricity-use goal, so this plan does not cover it.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Standard efficiency package (the efficiency measures are LED and controls): about 23,254 to 66,012 kWh a year, or 6% to 18% of use, after counting only 62% to 88% of the predicted savings because the City's own audited projects delivered that share. The underlying 10-20% saving is a planning estimate, not a measured figure.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Lighting type, cooling type, building controls and efficiency work already done were not entered. The plan assumes no efficiency work is in place. If LED lighting or controls are already installed, savings and their confidence drop, and those measures should not be repeated.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Usable roof: 32,860 sq ft x 0.55 is about 18,073 sq ft.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Whole-roof array size: about 274 kW DC. Because 11.4 kW already exists, the free roof fits about 262.4 kW DC of new solar. The roof is flat, so sizing rules apply.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: New 262.4 kW array output: about 314,134 to 345,150 kWh a year (middle about 329,667), tilted 10 degrees facing south, in typical-year weather. The range comes from the assumed loss band.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full free-roof array alone is about 88% of annual use at the middle output.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Rooftop solar alone is about 84% to 92% of annual use under the model, which reaches the 30% goal by itself on paper. That share is far above the usual 15-25%, so the roof area (which matches the footprint of all four buildings on the lot) and the structure must be verified before relying on it.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Gross solar bill savings for the 262.4 kW array: about $62,230 to $83,457 a year at the New York commercial average price range of 19.8 to 24.2 cents per kWh. This is the state average, not the building's own tariff.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario A, efficiency only: 21% to 59% of the goal (6.2% to 17.6% of use); does not reach the goal. Upfront cost typical range $65,824 to $226,165 (median of similar NYC projects about $144,025); net cost the same, no incentive counted; simple payback 4.1 to 49.1 years (median-cost case about 14 years); budget strain: within budget; outage hours: none, no backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency plus solar within budget (about 140 kW): 169% to 222% of the goal (50.8% to 66.6% of use); reaches the goal. Upfront cost typical range $418,771 to $750,000 (median about $562,870); net cost $312,887 to $592,849 (median about $437,217) with the federal credit counted; simple payback 5.2 to 15.7 years (median-cost case about 8.9); budget strain: within budget, using 56% to 100% of it; outage hours: none, no backup power.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C, full path (deep efficiency, 262.4 kW and a 203 kWh battery): 310% to 333% of the goal (93.1% to 100% of use); reaches the goal. Upfront cost typical range $855,950 to $1,436,661 (median about $1,113,444); net cost $623,694 to $1,091,853 (median about $835,446) with the federal credit counted; simple payback 6.9 to 15.8 years (median-cost case about 10.5); budget strain: over budget; outage hours 8.0 to 9.4.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario C costs $105,950 to $686,661 more than your budget and reaches the goal. Meeting the goal with backup may take more than the amount set aside; whether to extend it is the owner's decision.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Surplus solar: in Scenario C the roof could produce up to about 52,598 kWh a year more than the building still uses. That potential flows to the grid but is not counted in the savings, because export credits depend on net-metering rules that were not checked. No reduction above 100% is claimed.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The budget is entered as a capital amount for 2027; the model treats it as one total upfront figure, and payback is a simple payback, not the full SAM model.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Recommended scenario B, standard efficiency package: typical range $65,824 to $226,165 (median of similar NYC projects about $144,025). Basis: 56,260 kWh saved a year x $1.17-4.02 per kWh saved, from the middle half of completed NYC public-sector efficiency projects (NYSERDA data).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B rooftop solar: typical range $352,947 to $523,835 (median about $418,845). Basis: 139.6 kW DC x $2,528-3,752 per kW, from the middle half of 239 completed NYC non-residential projects of 100-500 kW since 2022 (NYSERDA data). This is a real price range, not a quote.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B federal credit line: minus $105,884 to minus $157,151 (30% of solar), counted only because the program page reads open. The page says governmental entities can receive the credit as a direct payment, solar must be placed in service by 2027-12-31, and whether this agency qualifies is not confirmed. Upfront cost before the credit is the safer figure for budgeting.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Full path (Scenario C) lines: expanded efficiency $81,764 to $287,301 (median about $186,783); solar 262.4 kW $663,347 to $984,525 (median about $787,200); battery 203 kWh at $546-812 per kWh, $110,838 to $164,836 (median about $139,461, from the middle half of 56 NYC storage projects, NYSERDA data); federal credit minus $232,256 to minus $344,808.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Federal elective pay (direct pay) for governmental entities is listed as open on the IRS page, with a deadline of 2027-12-31 for solar placed in service, read 2026-10-19. A budget year of 2027 leaves little time; confirm eligibility and timing before relying on it.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The NYSERDA NY-Sun commercial solar incentive status could not be confirmed from an official page, so it is uncertain and is left out of net cost. Check the NYSERDA dashboard in a browser.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: NYC Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019 are rules, not incentives: certain major roof renovations require a solar or green roof system. If roof work is planned, check whether they apply.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: None of the cost totals include repairing or replacing the roof. The roof's age and condition are unknown (the city record gave no roof details for this building, built 1936), so a roofer's quote is needed.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Phase 0, confirm data and budget: gather 12 months of Con Edison bills, confirm the $750,000 is a one-time capital amount for 2027, confirm the tariff on a bill, and confirm floor area, roof area and street address.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed professional engineer (PE) or registered architect (RA) for structural analysis, plus a roof condition survey. The roof cannot be certified from these records.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 2, efficiency measures: standard package (LED and controls, unless already installed), with cooling-center gym cooling checked first; about 6% to 18% of use.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 3, permits and interconnection: Department of Buildings permits, Landmarks Preservation Commission review, a Con Edison interconnection application, a licensed electrician, and FDNY rooftop access review.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 4, solar installation: about 140 kW within budget (Scenario B), growing toward the full 262.4 kW later if the budget is extended.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: add a flood-protected battery sized from a metered critical load, then check results against bills. The full-path scenario prices a 203 kWh battery at $110,838 to $164,836; a smaller or phased battery was not priced separately.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario C gives about 8.0 to 9.4 hours of backup for the critical loads (gym cooling, lighting and communications for a cooling center). Scenarios A and B give no backup power: solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A4: the battery (203 kWh, 21.6 kW) rests on an estimated critical load of 1.0 W per sq ft and an assumed 8-hour backup; neither was entered or metered. Gym cooling for a cooling center may need more power, so the real size could be larger.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The current FEMA flood map places this address in zone AE (a special flood hazard area), and the site flooded in Hurricane Sandy. Put the battery, inverters and switchgear on the roof or elevate them above the design flood elevation.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Only the current flood zone was read. Heat and winter-storm ratings were not looked up, and the 2015 preliminary flood map, which NYC code also considers, was not checked.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Backup needs inverters able to run the building while the grid is down; the electrician and Con Edison interconnection review should confirm this.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Structural analysis by a licensed PE or RA and a roof condition survey are required. The roof cannot be certified from these records, and this plan does not replace that review.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: A licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review and a Con Edison interconnection review are required for any solar or battery work.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Flood-zone review under NYC Building Code Appendix G is needed because the site is in zone AE.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The city record carries a landmark flag, so a Landmarks Preservation Commission review is needed before any rooftop or exterior work. Because the building is on city parkland, the Commission gives the owning agency an advisory report, not a permit.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Parkland use review by counsel, and NYC Parks as the owning agency, are part of the approval route.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: The roof area, pitch, direction, shading and structure are all items to verify with an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

sections.title: Path to net-zero and learning resources

claims.text: The full path (Scenario C) is estimated to cover about 93% to 100% of grid electricity use, so it is the closest option to net-zero electricity, but it does not cover natural gas heating.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The City's Local Law 87 report is a useful guide to how much predicted efficiency savings audited city projects actually delivered.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city lists the lot under 140 Lorraine Street, not 155 Bay Street. Both addresses are shown; confirm they are the same lot, since the building records may not be for this exact frontage.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Floor area: 21,600 sq ft entered and in the lot record, against 27,069 sq ft in the city energy report. The entered value is the working figure; please confirm.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The year the roof was replaced, roof condition, owning-agency details, lighting type, cooling type, building controls, heating fuel, critical load in kW, desired backup hours and electricity price were not entered. These are unknown, and claims that depend on them have lower confidence. The city roof record also gave no roof condition or age.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The electricity price is the New York commercial average (19.8 to 24.2 cents per kWh), not this building's tariff. The tariff must be confirmed on a bill; the utility lists several general-service tariffs (published effective 2025-02-01) and none is chosen here.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The incentive list is a curated register kept by a person, with each official page re-read on 2026-10-19. The NY-Sun incentive could not be confirmed and is left out. Federal credit eligibility for this agency is not confirmed.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Only the flood zone was read; heat and storm ratings and the 2015 preliminary map were not checked. The battery size comes from estimated, not metered, inputs. Efficiency savings percents are planning estimates, not project data.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: No other conflicts were found between cached and live data, and no retrieved page carried hidden instructions.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Main data sources: NYC Open Data building records (lot, footprints, Local Law 84 and 24), PVWatts solar model, EIA electricity prices, NYSERDA project cost data, FEMA flood map and the IRS elective pay page. The system adds the full list of links below the plan.
claims.label: FACT

roadmap.footer_note: All figures are estimate ranges for planning, not quotes or promises of savings.
roadmap.plain_answer: You asked how to cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages on $750,000. The plan estimates the 30% goal can be reached within your budget: standard efficiency work plus a budget-sized rooftop solar array (about 140 kW) cuts roughly 51% to 67% of grid use, while efficiency alone reaches only about 6% to 18%. Outage backup is the gap. Only the full path with a battery gives backup, about 8 to 9 hours, and it costs $105,950 to $686,661 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is your decision. The building already has 11.4 kW of solar, and the baseline is electricity bought from the grid. Several records do not line up: the city lists the lot under 140 Lorraine Street, the energy report shows 27,069 sq ft against your 21,600, and your roof area equals the ground footprint of all four buildings on the lot. Next, have an engineer or roofer confirm the usable roof, then meter the real critical load and ask for the price of adding a flood-protected battery to the within-budget plan.
